U.S. Navy · Fast Battleships · 1943–1992

TheIowa Class

The last and greatest battleships America ever built. Six were ordered, four were finished — and those four fought in World War II, Korea, Vietnam and the Gulf War across five decades. This is every ship of the class: the legends, and the two that never sailed.

Built to outrun everything

The Class

Earlier battleships were built to slug it out in a line of battle. The Iowas were built for speed: at 33 knots they could keep up with the new fast aircraft carriers, escort them, and still outgun anything afloat. Their beam — 108 feet — was set by one hard limit: they had to fit through the Panama Canal's 110-foot locks, with about a foot to spare on each side.

A floating anti-aircraft fortress

In 1943 the Iowas bristled with guns of every size — the nine big rifles for surface battle, and a forest of smaller weapons to throw up a wall of fire against kamikazes and dive bombers.

  • 16-inch / 50 Mark 7 rifles9
  • 5-inch / 38 dual-purpose guns20
  • 40 mm Bofors anti-aircraft80
  • 20 mm Oerlikon anti-aircraft49
  • OS2U Kingfisher floatplanes3
  • TorpedoesNone — ever

Missiles on a battleship hull

Brought back under President Reagan's 600-ship Navy, all four were rebuilt with cruise missiles, modern radar and electronic warfare gear. Four of the ten 5-inch mounts were removed to make room — the 16-inch guns stayed exactly where they'd always been.

  • 16-inch / 50 Mark 7 rifles9
  • 5-inch / 38 dual-purpose guns12
  • BGM-109 Tomahawk cruise missiles32
  • RGM-84 Harpoon anti-ship missiles16
  • Phalanx close-in weapon systems4
  • RQ-2 Pioneer spotting dronesCarried
24,300 LB

One broadside. Each 16-inch armour-piercing shell weighed 2,700 lb — about as much as a Volkswagen Beetle — and could be thrown roughly 23 miles. Fire all nine guns together and a single salvo put over twelve tons of steel in the air.

BB-61 · Iowa

Lead ship of the class

USS Iowa

“The Big Stick”
Museum ship · Los Angeles, California

The first of the class, and the only one to ferry a president to a wartime summit. In November 1943 Iowa carried Franklin D. Roosevelt across the Atlantic to the Tehran Conference — a bathtub was installed aboard for him, the only one ever fitted on a U.S. Navy ship, and the elevator she still carries was put in for his wheelchair.

She went on to shell Japanese positions across the Pacific, bombard Korea twice over, and return in the 1980s as a Cold War showpiece. Her career also holds the class's darkest day: on 19 April 1989, an explosion in Turret Two during gunnery exercises killed 47 sailors. The turret was never repaired, and its hatch remains sealed.

BuilderNew York Naval Shipyard
Laid down27 June 1940
Commissioned22 February 1943
Battle stars11 — 9 WWII, 2 Korea
Final decommission26 October 1990
Museum since7 July 2012

Claim to fame

During the run to Tehran, the destroyer William D. Porter accidentally fired a live torpedo at Iowa — with the President aboard. It exploded harmlessly in her wake. Roosevelt, told a torpedo was coming, asked to be wheeled to the rail so he could watch.

BB-62 · New Jersey

Most decorated battleship in U.S. history

USS New Jersey

“Black Dragon”
Museum ship · Camden, New Jersey

No American battleship fought more. New Jersey earned 19 battle and campaign stars — more than any other battleship in U.S. Navy history — across an unmatched run of wars: the Pacific in WWII, Korea, and then a fight all her own.

In 1968 she became the only battleship to serve in the Vietnam War, recalled alone to shell the coast while her sisters slept. Brought back again in 1982, she bombarded positions in Lebanon in 1983–84 — the last time her 16-inch guns were fired in anger before the Gulf era — and served longer in commission than any of her sisters.

BuilderPhiladelphia Naval Shipyard
Laid down16 September 1940
Launched7 Dec 1942 — a year after Pearl Harbor
Commissioned23 May 1943
Battle stars19 — a Navy battleship record
Final decommission8 February 1991

Claim to fame

Four separate careers: WWII, Korea, Vietnam and the Cold War. She is the only one of the four to have fought in Vietnam — and the only U.S. battleship ever recommissioned for that war.

BB-63 · Missouri

Where World War II ended

USS Missouri

“Mighty Mo”
Museum ship · Pearl Harbor, Hawaii

On the morning of 2 September 1945, on Missouri's deck in Tokyo Bay, Japanese officials signed the Instrument of Surrender and World War II officially ended. A brass plaque marks the exact spot. She had been named for the home state of President Harry Truman — and christened by his daughter Margaret.

She was the last battleship the U.S. ever commissioned (11 June 1944) and, 48 years later, the last active battleship in the world. In between: Korean War bombardments, an embarrassing 1950 grounding in Chesapeake Bay that took two weeks to pull her off, and a final war in 1991, when she launched Tomahawk strikes in the opening of Desert Storm and spotted her own gunfire with a Pioneer drone — Iraqi soldiers on Faylaka Island famously tried to surrender to the drone.

BuilderNew York Naval Shipyard
Laid down6 January 1941
Commissioned11 June 1944
Battle stars11 — WWII, Korea, Gulf
Final decommission31 March 1992
Museum since29 January 1999

Bookends of a war

At Pearl Harbor she moors a short distance from the sunken USS Arizona, lost in the attack that started the war for America. Together the two ships bookend it: Arizona where it began, Missouri where it ended.

BB-64 · Wisconsin

The last one launched

USS Wisconsin

“Wisky” — part Kentucky
Museum ship · Norfolk, Virginia

Launched on 7 December 1943 — two years to the day after Pearl Harbor — Wisconsin raced through WWII earning five battle stars, shelled Korea, and in the Gulf War fired Tomahawks and ran her own Pioneer drone spotting, just like Missouri.

Her strangest chapter came in peacetime. On 6 May 1956 she collided with the destroyer USS Eaton, crushing 68 feet of her bow. The Navy's fix: cut the bow off her unfinished sister Kentucky and graft it on. The transplant worked — and earned her the hybrid nickname “WisKy.” She sails today, as a museum, still wearing Kentucky's bow.

BuilderPhiladelphia Naval Shipyard
Laid down25 January 1941
Launched7 Dec 1943 — two years after Pearl Harbor
Commissioned16 April 1944
Battle stars6 — 5 WWII, 1 Korea
Final decommission30 September 1991

Claim to fame

The only battleship in the world sailing with another ship's bow. When you stand at Wisconsin's forecastle in Norfolk, the steel under your feet was built for BB-66, Kentucky.

The two that never sailed

BB-65 & BB-66

Six Iowas were ordered. Four were finished. These two were cancelled as the war ended — but one of them still managed to donate a piece of herself to a sister.

BB-65

USS Illinois

Her keel was laid at Philadelphia on 15 January 1945, in the war's final months. Work crawled as victory approached, and on 12 August 1945 — days before Japan's surrender — she was cancelled outright. The partial hull sat in the shipyard for thirteen years before being broken up for scrap in 1958.

Completed~22%

Fate: Cancelled 1945 · Scrapped 1958 · Never launched. Her name went unused by a U.S. battleship until the submarine era.

BB-66

USS Kentucky

Her keel was first laid at Norfolk on 6 June 1942, then work was suspended almost at once while the yard built carriers and escorts; construction resumed in December 1944. Kentucky got much further than her sister — about 72% complete when work stopped for good in 1946. She was launched in 1950 for the least glamorous reason imaginable: the Navy needed her dry dock empty. Plans to finish her as a guided-missile battleship (BBG-1) were drawn up and dropped, twice.

Completed~72%

Fate: Sold for scrap, October 1958 — but her bow lives on, grafted onto USS Wisconsin after the 1956 collision. Part of BB-66 is still afloat today.

Fifty years of service

Timeline
1940–41

Keels laid

All four completed ships are laid down in New York and Philadelphia as America rearms. Two more hulls, Illinois and Kentucky, are authorised behind them.

1943

Iowa carries a president

Iowa commissions first and ferries President Roosevelt to the Tehran Conference. New Jersey follows her into the Pacific as a carrier-task-force flagship.

2 SEP 1945

The war ends on Missouri's deck

Japan signs the Instrument of Surrender aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. Weeks earlier, BB-65 Illinois had been cancelled with the war already won.

1950–53

Korea

All four sisters are recalled to shell the Korean coast. Kentucky, meanwhile, is launched only to free her dry dock, her future already in doubt.

1956

The bow transplant

Wisconsin collides with the destroyer Eaton. Her crushed bow is replaced with the bow of the unfinished Kentucky — the class's most unusual repair.

1968–69

New Jersey goes to Vietnam alone

The only battleship recommissioned for Vietnam, New Jersey fires nearly 6,000 16-inch shells at the coast in a single deployment.

1982–88

The missile-age rebuild

All four return under the 600-ship Navy, rearmed with Tomahawk and Harpoon missiles. New Jersey shells Lebanon; the class becomes a Cold War symbol.

19 APR 1989

Tragedy on Iowa

An explosion in Turret Two kills 47 of Iowa's crew during exercises off Puerto Rico. The turret is sealed and never repaired.

1991

Last shots: Desert Storm

Missouri and Wisconsin launch Tomahawk strikes and shell Kuwait — the final combat deployment of any battleship, nearly 50 years after the class was designed.

31 MAR 1992

The era ends

Missouri, the last active battleship in the world, decommissions at Long Beach. All four sisters pass to museums — where all four remain today.

You can walk their decks

Visit Them

All four finished ships survive as museums — the only battleship class in the world you can still visit in full. Each one is worth the trip for a different reason.

BB-61 · West Coast

Battleship IOWA Museum

San Pedro, Los Angeles, California

See the President's bathtub, the sealed Turret Two, and the bridge Roosevelt crossed the Atlantic from.

BB-62 · East Coast

Battleship New Jersey

Camden, New Jersey

The most decorated of the four, moored across the Delaware River from Philadelphia, where she was built.

BB-63 · Pacific

Battleship Missouri Memorial

Pearl Harbor, Honolulu, Hawaii

Stand on the Surrender Deck, then look across the harbour to the USS Arizona Memorial — the war's beginning and end in one view.

BB-64 · East Coast

USS Wisconsin at Nauticus

Downtown Norfolk, Virginia

Walk the longest main deck of the four in the middle of the world's largest naval town — and stand on Kentucky's bow.

Ship histories follow the U.S. Navy's Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships (DANFS) entries for each vessel. Photographs: the in-service shots — USS Iowa's broadside, USS New Jersey in Korea and off Vietnam, and USS Missouri and USS Wisconsin underway — are U.S. Navy photos (public domain, via Wikimedia Commons and the U.S. National Archives); museum photographs show the ships at their present berths in Los Angeles, Pearl Harbor and Norfolk.

The four completed ships remain the property of history and their museum foundations — and all four can still be toured today.
